problem: The answer says HL and DE can be swapped with three MOV instructions taking three bytes. Two 8-bit registers cannot be swapped with three moves: each byte needs a temporary, and A can hold only one byte at a time. The real sequence is six MOVs (MOV A,H / MOV H,D / MOV D,A / MOV A,L / MOV L,E / MOV E,A), that is six bytes and six instructions. A student who writes 'three MOVs' loses marks.
fix: XCHG takes one byte and one instruction; the equivalent MOV sequence needs six MOV instructions and six bytes (A used twice as the temporary), so XCHG saves five bytes and five instructions.

problem: The second reason given is not a difference: MOV also leaves all five flags unchanged on the 8085, so 'XCHG leaves the flags unchanged' cannot be a reason to prefer XCHG over MOVs.
fix: Replace the second reason with a real one: the MOV sequence must use A as a temporary and destroys its old value, while XCHG swaps HL and DE without disturbing A, B, C, D, E or the flags.

problem: 'A memory-to-memory copy would also need two bus cycles' is loose. A single instruction reading and writing memory needs two separate memory accesses (a read machine cycle and a write machine cycle), each several T-states long.
fix: A memory-to-memory copy would need two memory accesses, one read and one write, in the same instruction, so the encoding was not offered; opcode 76H is used for HLT.

problem: 'HL is not allowed because [HL] already has the name M' and 'HL has no 16-bit form here' are misleading. HL is a 16-bit register pair; the actual reason is that no LDAX H / STAX H opcode exists, because MOV A,M and MOV M,A already do that job.
fix: LDAX and STAX exist only for BC and DE. There is no LDAX H or STAX H opcode, and none is needed, since MOV A,M and MOV M,A already copy between A and the byte at HL.
